strengths: Addresses an important gap in dynamical systems reconstruction: a continuous-time piecewise-linear RNN that enables irregular sampling and arbitrary-time interpolation while retaining mathematical tractability.

Introduces a nontrivial algorithmic pipeline combining analytic solutions within linear regions, interval-based branch-and-prune root finding for switching times, and custom implicit differentiation through switching times.
Demonstrates practical speed advantages over Neural ODEs on Lorenz-63 and LIF benchmarks (roughly 2–7x faster training) with comparable reconstruction performance.
Shows a clear empirical advantage over discrete-time PLRNN on irregularly sampled LIF data, where the discrete model breaks down.

Provides semi-analytical tools for post-hoc analysis of trained models, including fixed points via an adapted SCYFI and limit cycles via a system of equations, with illustrative examples on Lorenz-63, LIF, and real neuron data.
Includes an honest limitations section acknowledging numerical robustness issues and scaling concerns.
weaknesses: Missing critical ablation: the paper claims its solver is more efficient and precise than numerical integration, but never compares cPLRNN trained with the proposed solver against cPLRNN trained with a numerical ODE solver on the same vector field. The runtime comparison against Neural ODEs confounds model architecture and solver, so the central solver-efficiency claim is not directly supported.

Limited empirical evaluation: only three low-dimensional benchmarks (Lorenz-63, LIF, single-neuron recording). No high-dimensional or more challenging real-world datasets, and no comparison to other continuous-time DSR methods such as latent ODEs, neural CDEs, ODE-RNNs, or rSLDS. The Neural ODE baseline architecture is not fully specified, raising fairness concerns.

Theoretical gaps: no formal guarantees for the root-finding algorithm's correctness, termination, or complexity. Limit cycle detection requires an initial guess of the region sequence and time estimates, with no described strategy for obtaining these or guarantees of finding all cycles. Sliding modes, tangential crossings, and simultaneous boundary crossings are not discussed.

Performance is not state-of-the-art: on regularly sampled data, cPLRNN is often slightly worse than discrete PLRNN and not consistently better than Neural ODEs. The main practical advantages are speed and irregular sampling, making the contribution narrower than the framing suggests.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or data availability statement. The custom root finder and interval arithmetic implementation lack sufficient detail (tolerances, splitting strategy, maximum iterations) for exact reproduction. Data for the real neuron recordings may not be publicly available.

Presentation issues: numerous typos, inconsistent citations (e.g., wrong years, duplicated references), a malformed appendix section B.2 with corrupted tensor notation, and unclear statistical reporting (e.g., 'all p > 0.048' for non-significance).

Statistical analysis is underpowered: 10 runs per condition, no correction for multiple comparisons, and some conclusions rely on p-values near 0.05 (e.g., p < 0.043, p > 0.048). Effect sizes and uncertainty are not adequately discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: all existing PLRNN/ALRNN variants are discrete-time maps and therefore cannot naturally handle irregularly sampled data, while the natural continuous-time alternative (Neural ODEs) is slower and less interpretable. A continuous-time PLRNN is a well-motivated target.

The technical machinery is plausible: per-subregion analytic solutions (Eq. 6-7), switching-time detection via a custom interval-Newton branch-and-prune scheme, and implicit-function-theorem gradients through switch times form a coherent pipeline, and the parallelizable within-region evaluation (Algorithm 1) is a real conceptual advantage over sequential integration.

The state-space analysis section is a useful addition, showing how equilibria (via an adaptation of SCYFI to Eq. 13) and limit cycles (Eq. 14) can be recovered semi-analytically, and Figure 1/2 illustrate this on Lorenz-63, LIF, and empirical membrane recordings.

The irregular-sampling experiment (Table 3, right) is the one clear empirical win: the standard discrete PLRNN essentially collapses (D_step ~4.3) whereas the cPLRNN remains competitive, which directly demonstrates the intended practical benefit.
The limitations section is honest about numerical robustness, ill-conditioned eigen-decompositions, and the cost of restarting root finding after each switching event.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty is overstated. Event detection / switching-time computation for piecewise-linear and hybrid systems is a mature topic (Bemporad et al., Coombes et al., Avrutin et al., and the authors' own cited hybrid-systems literature). The 'novel algorithm' reduces to (a) an analytic solution per linear region, which is textbook for linear ODEs, and (b) interval-Newton root finding modeled after IntervalRootFinding.jl. The framing as 'bypassing numerical integration' is misleading, since root finding is itself a numerical procedure; what is avoided is adaptive step-size integration, not numerics.

There is no demonstrated performance advantage. Tables 1, 3, and 4 consistently show the cPLRNN matching or slightly trailing the baselines: on Lorenz-63 it is 'slightly worse' than the standard PLRNN (p<0.043) and only 'on par' with Tsit5; on LIF-regular it is on par; on membrane recordings it is on par with the standard PLRNN (p>0.07) and only marginally better than Neural ODE. The paper's central contribution therefore amounts to parity, not improvement, which undercuts the motivation.

The runtime comparison (Table 2) is confounded. cPLRNN (21-36 s) is faster than Neural ODE (39-175 s), but the standard PLRNN is an order of magnitude faster (4.7-5.1 s), and the Neural ODE and cPLRNN use different parameterizations (diagonal A, structured W) so the timings do not isolate the effect of the solver.

Reproducibility is weak. The custom interval-Newton root finder is complex and not released; training is admitted to be numerically fragile (ill-conditioned eigen-decompositions, rare divergences), and the boundary-crossing fix relies on an ad hoc perturbation dt=0.0001 that the authors explicitly say is 'still an open question'. This makes it hard for others to build on the method.

The limit-cycle machinery (Eq. 14) requires an a priori guess of the region sequence R and initial estimates of {T_i} and y, then a Trust-Region/Variable-Projection solve. This is a significant practical limitation that is not stress-tested, and it is unclear how the region sequence is obtained for high-dimensional systems.

Scalability concerns are not addressed: the state space has 2^P regions, and the paper concedes that root finding must restart after each switching event, increasing cost for models with many boundaries. No experiments probe larger P beyond 10.

The baseline set is thin. Only Neural ODEs (three solvers) and the discrete PLRNN are compared; there is no comparison to latent Neural ODEs / Neural CDEs (which are the standard tools for irregularly sampled series), nor to other continuous piecewise-linear or hybrid-system identification methods, so the claim of being the appropriate solution is not substantiated against the most relevant competitors.

Statistical support is thin: 10 runs with Mann-Whitney tests yield borderline p-values (e.g., 'all p>0.048', 'p<0.043'), giving low power, and several cells report only 2-6 valid runs (Euler divergences), which further weakens the comparisons.

Presentation has numerous errors: duplicated figure captions ('A) Top: ...' twice in Figure 2), citation year mismatches (e.g., 'Brenner et al. (2022)' used for a 2024 paper; Chen et al. 2018 indexed as 2018 but some references mis-dated), typos ('specical', 'looses out performance-wise', 'in disaccord'), and a malformed Table 5 column layout, all of which impede readability.

strengths: Introduces a novel continuous-time piecewise-linear RNN (cPLRNN) and an algorithm that exploits the PL structure to solve the ODE semi-analytically via switching-time detection, avoiding standard numerical integration.

Provides a principled way to compute topological properties (equilibria, limit cycles) of trained models by adapting PL dynamical systems theory, enhancing interpretability beyond black-box Neural ODEs.

Empirical results on Lorenz-63, LIF, and real neuron recordings show cPLRNN is competitive with Neural ODEs and significantly better on irregularly sampled LIF data, while training several times faster than Neural ODEs.

The theoretical derivations (region-wise solutions, implicit differentiation through switching times, interval Newton root finding) are mathematically sound and well-grounded in the PL systems literature.
The limitations section is honest about numerical robustness and scaling issues, and the paper uses standard DSR evaluation metrics (Dstep, DH, MAE).
weaknesses: The claimed precision advantage of the semi-analytical solver over numerical integration is not directly validated; there is no comparison of forward-simulation error against high-accuracy ODE solvers.

Topological analysis is demonstrated only qualitatively (visual overlays of fixed points and limit cycles) without quantitative accuracy metrics, and limit cycle detection requires manual initial guesses of the region sequence.

The irregular-sampling advantage is mainly shown against a discrete PLRNN that must interpolate the data; no comparison to continuous-time models designed for irregular data (e.g., Latent ODE, Neural CDE) is provided.

Scalability and robustness are insufficiently evaluated: experiments use small M and P (≤10), root finding restarts after every switch, a fixed δt=0.0001 perturbation is used, and ill-conditioned eigendecompositions can cause training failures.
Reproducibility is limited: the Neural ODE baseline architecture and the handling of sparse teacher forcing for irregular time points are not fully specified, and no code is released.

The cPLRNN is a continuous PL system and cannot exactly represent discontinuous/impact systems such as the LIF neuron with reset; using LIF as a discontinuity benchmark without discussing this model-class mismatch is conceptually questionable.

Statistical evidence is weak due to small n=10, use of non-parametric tests without effect sizes, and several p-values close to 0.05; on regularly sampled Lorenz, the discrete PLRNN often outperforms cPLRNN.
The paper contains numerous reference errors and typos (e.g., wrong years, author names), which hinder presentation quality.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: continuous-time dynamical systems reconstruction that is both performant and mathematically tractable, especially for irregularly sampled data.
Proposes a semi-analytical solver for piecewise-linear ODEs that avoids numerical integration within linear subregions, using an interval Newton root finder to locate switching times.
Provides a method for differentiating through switching times via the implicit function theorem, enabling gradient-based training of the proposed model.
Extends topological analysis (fixed points, limit cycles) to continuous-time PL RNNs, with concrete algorithms and illustrative examples on Lorenz-63, LIF, and real neuron data.
Empirical results show cPLRNN matches or exceeds Neural ODE performance on several benchmarks, with faster training times, and handles irregular sampling better than discrete-time PLRNN.
Code is available and hyperparameters are provided, supporting reproducibility.
Includes a limitations section that acknowledges numerical robustness and scaling issues.
weaknesses: Lacks positioning relative to the extensive literature on continuous-time threshold-linear networks (TLNs) and event-driven simulation of piecewise-linear systems; the cPLRNN is essentially a TLN, and its fixed-point analysis is closely related to known combinatorial results, undermining claimed novelty.

Experimental design does not isolate the contribution of the proposed solver: comparisons are between cPLRNN (PL model with custom solver) and Neural ODEs (MLP vector fields with numerical solvers). A proper baseline would be the same cPLRNN trained with numerical integration (e.g., adaptive ODE solver with event detection) to demonstrate the advantage of bypassing integration.

No direct evaluation of the accuracy or efficiency of the proposed root-finding algorithm compared to alternatives (e.g., dense-output event detection, standard root finders); the claim of being 'much more efficient and precise' is not quantitatively supported.

The gradient computation through switching times is not validated (e.g., no gradient check, no comparison to finite differences), and the paper does not fully detail how the gradient of the state at the switching time with respect to parameters accounts for the dependence on the switching time, raising concerns about correctness.

Topological analysis (fixed points, limit cycles) is demonstrated qualitatively but not quantitatively evaluated; no error metrics for detected fixed points/limit cycles, and no comparison to ground truth or alternative methods. The claim of 'exact' location is overstated.
The model assumes invertible and diagonalizable W_{Omega^k}, and the handling of non-diagonalizable cases via perturbation is heuristic; no analysis of how often this occurs or its impact.
Presentation inconsistencies: 'D_step' vs 'D_stsp' naming, repeated headers, and some figures referenced but not clearly shown in the main text; minor but affects readability.

Reproducibility is partially limited: the exact application of sparse teacher forcing to irregularly sampled data is not clearly specified, training hardware and software versions are not fully reported, and the code URL is truncated.
The limitations section omits the most important limitations: lack of comparison to numerical integration of the same model, lack of gradient verification, and incomplete discussion of related work.

Empirical gains over Neural ODEs are modest and often not statistically significant; the main advantage is speed, but the discrete PLRNN remains faster and often better on regularly sampled data, so the practical benefit is mainly for irregular sampling, where a Neural ODE with a good solver might also suffice.

strengths: Introduces a continuous-time piecewise-linear RNN (cPLRNN) that naturally handles irregularly sampled data and arbitrary-time interpolation, addressing a genuine limitation of discrete-time PLRNNs.

Provides a semi-analytic solver for PL ODEs by locating switching times with an interval-Newton branch-and-prune method, avoiding generic numerical integration; demonstrates faster training than RK4/Tsit5 on Lorenz and competitive DSR performance on several benchmarks.

Shows how to adapt existing tools (SCYFI, Coombes et al.) to semi-analytically detect fixed points and limit cycles in trained cPLRNNs, with illustrative examples on Lorenz-63, LIF, and cortical recordings.
Code and hyperparameters are provided, and the paper includes an honest limitations section covering numerical robustness, root-finding restarts, and shallow architectures.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: analytic solutions per linear subregion and switching-time computation are standard in piecewise-smooth/hybrid systems; the core algorithm adapts known techniques (interval Newton from IntervalRootFinding.jl, SCYFI, Coombes et al.) rather than introducing fundamentally new theory.

Empirical comparisons are not always fair or fully specified: the Neural ODE architecture (layers, parameterization) is not described; the Lorenz time axis is scaled by 100 while the discrete PLRNN uses dt=0.01; for irregular LIF the continuous model uses sequence length 20 but the standard PLRNN uses 200, confounding the comparison.

Central claims of 'much more efficient and precise' are not fully supported: precision is never compared to numerical integration; training-time advantage is only ~3x vs Tsit5 and ~1.3x vs Euler (which is competitive on regular LIF), and grows with P; no error-vs-cost analysis is provided.

Critical methodological details are missing: the full gradient propagation through the root finder and multiple switching events is not derived (the implicit function theorem only gives the derivative of a single switching time); the interval extension of f' needed for interval Newton is not specified; and the perturbation δt=0.0001 used to cross boundaries is an admitted hack with unclear effect on dynamics.

The method assumes invertible, diagonalizable W_{Ω^k}; when violated, it perturbs the matrix and discards gradient contributions, but the frequency and impact of these cases are not analyzed, potentially biasing training.

State-space analysis is only demonstrated on a few examples; there is no quantitative evaluation of detection accuracy, false positives/negatives, or comparison of found cycles/fixed points against ground truth across many systems.

Performance does not consistently surpass existing methods: on Lorenz, standard PLRNN is significantly better (p<0.043) and Neural ODE Tsit5 is better on D_step/D_H; on regular LIF, Neural ODE Euler is better; cPLRNN's clear advantage is mainly for irregular sampling versus discrete PLRNN, but Neural ODEs also handle irregular sampling and remain competitive.

The limitations discussion omits several important issues, including unfair benchmark settings, missing gradient details, scalability to larger P, and the impact of assumption violations, so it is incomplete.

strengths: Introduces the first continuous-time piecewise-linear RNN (cPLRNN), a well-motivated and genuinely new model class that bridges the mathematical tractability of PLRNNs with the continuous-time nature of Neural ODEs, enabling evaluation at arbitrary time points and handling of irregularly sampled data (Sect. 1, 3.1).

The core algorithm is technically sound: within each linear subregion the flow has a closed-form solution (Eq. 6-7), switching times are located with a purpose-built interval-Newton branch-and-prune root finder that guarantees finding the *first* root (Sect. C, Algorithm 2), and gradients through the switching times are correctly derived via the implicit function theorem (Eq. 11-12). Computing all states within a subregion in parallel (Algorithm 1) is a clean efficiency win over sequential integration.

A concrete and demonstrated computational benefit: Table 2 shows cPLRNN trains roughly 3x faster than the best Neural ODE solver (Tsit5; ~33s vs ~107s at P=10) while matching DSR performance, and Fig. 8 provides scaling analysis of runtime with M and P.

The semi-analytic analysis tools are a real value-add for scientific use: fixed points are found by adapting SCYFI to the continuous fixed-point equation (Eq. 13), and limit cycles are obtained as exact solutions of a well-posed root-finding system (Eq. 14) with demonstrated robustness to initialization (Fig. 7) and low runtimes (<15s).

Evaluation is broad and statistically grounded: four benchmarks (Lorenz-63, LIF, cortical membrane potential, PhysioNet heartbeats), comparisons to Neural ODEs under three solvers, discrete PLRNN, Latent ODE, Neural CDE and SINDy, with 10 runs and Mann-Whitney/Wilcoxon tests. The irregular-sampling advantage is convincingly shown (Tables 3, 7).

The limitations discussion is honest and specific (training instabilities from ill-conditioned eigendecompositions, δt perturbation, root-finding restarts, shallow-model scope), and the impact statement is appropriate.
weaknesses: The headline DSR performance is at parity, not superiority: on Lorenz-63 (Table 1) Neural ODE with Tsit5 is actually better on both D_step (0.30 vs 0.37) and D_H (0.085 vs 0.116), and on the irregular LIF benchmark cPLRNN is only comparable to Neural ODE RK4 on D_step (6.6 vs 6.2). The claim of a 'much more efficient and precise' solver is only partly supported—the precision advantage over adaptive integration is not isolated experimentally, and the compelling contrast is mainly against the discrete PLRNN, which is expected by design.

The main benefits (speed and tractability) are meaningful but modest: the discrete PLRNN remains ~7x faster per epoch (Table 2), and the practical gain over Neural ODEs is roughly a 3x speedup plus analytical fixed-point/limit-cycle extraction rather than a clear reconstruction-quality improvement.

Numerical reliability is a genuine concern for a method marketed as robust: training can terminate from ill-conditioned eigendecompositions, and the fixed perturbation δt=0.0001 used to force boundary crossings is explicitly acknowledged as an open problem that could jump across additional boundaries and alter dynamics (Sect. C.4, Appx. D.2).

Limit-cycle detection depends on a user-supplied initial guess of the region sequence and times of flight and may miss orbits; while the authors show robustness (Fig. 7), this inherits the initialization sensitivity of continuation methods and is not fully resolved.

The Neural CDE and Latent ODE comparisons contribute little: they are reported as best-over-runs rather than medians, and the authors themselves argue these models are unsuited to autonomous long-term rollouts, so the large reported gaps are largely expected and do not strengthen the central claims.

Reproducibility has a gap: the code availability line ('Code is available at') appears to have no actual link in the manuscript, and the Neural ODE baselines use a fixed solver Δt=1.0 (Table 6), which may not be an entirely fair configuration against an analytically solved model.
